'''Zhangzhung''' ({{bo|t=ཞང་ཞུང་|w=zhang zhung}}) is an [[extinct language|extinct]] [[Sino-Tibetan languages|Sino-Tibetan language]] that was spoken in [[Zhangzhung]] in what is now western [[Tibet]]. It is attested in a bilingual text called ''A Cavern of Treasures'' (''mDzod phug'') and several shorter texts.

A small number of documents preserved in [[Dunhuang manuscripts|Dunhuang]] contain an undeciphered language that has been called '''Old Zhangzhung''', but the identification is controversial.

==''A Cavern of Treasures'' (''mDzod phug'')==
''A Cavern of Treasures'' ({{bo|t=མཛོད་ཕུག་|w=mdzod phug}}) is a [[terma (religion)|terma]] uncovered by Shenchen Luga ({{bo|t=གཤེན་ཆེན་ཀླུ་དགའ་|w=gshen chen klu dga'}}) in the early eleventh century.<ref>Berzin, Alexander (2005). ''The Four Immeasurable Attitudes in Hinayana, Mahayana, and Bön.'' Study Buddhism. Source: [https://studybuddhism.com/en/advanced-studies/abhidharma-tenet-systems/comparison-of-buddhist-traditions/the-four-immeasurables-in-hinayana-mahayana-and-bon] (accessed: June 6, 2016)</ref> Martin identifies the importance of  this scripture for studies of the Zhangzhung language:{{blockquote|For students of Tibetan culture in general, the ''mDzod phug'' is one of the most intriguing of all Bön scriptures, since it is the only lengthy bilingual work in Zhang-zhung and Tibetan (some of the shorter but still significant sources for Zhang-zhung are signalled in Orofino 1990)."<ref>{{cite book |surname=Martin |given=Dan |chapter=Comparing Treasuries: Mental states and other ''mdzod phug'' lists and passages with parallels in Abhidharma works of Vasubandhu and Asanga, or in Prajnaparamita Sutras: A progress report |pages=21–88 |title=New Horizons in Bon Studies |editor1-given=S.G. |editor1-surname=Karmay |editor2-given=Y. |editor2-surname=Nagano |location=Osaka |publisher=National Museum of Ethnology |year=2000 |series=Senri Ethnological Reports |volume=15 |doi=10.15021/00002197 |doi-access=free }} p. 21.</ref>}}

==External relationships==

Bradley (2002) says Zhangzhung "is now agreed" to have been a Kanauri or [[West Himalayish languages|West Himalayish]] language. [[Guillaume Jacques]] (2009) rebuts earlier hypotheses that Zhangzhung might have originated in eastern (rather than western) Tibet by having determined it to be a non-[[Qiangic languages|Qiangic]] language.<ref>{{cite book |last=Jacques |first=Guillaume |chapter=Zhangzhung and Qiangic Languages |chapter-url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/halshs-00339148/document |type=PDF |title=Issues in Tibeto-Burman Historical Linguistics|series=Senri Ethnological Studies |volume=75 |pages=121–130 |editor=Yasuhiko Nagano |year=2009}}</ref>

Widmer (2014) classifies Zhangzhung within the eastern branch of West Himalayish, and lists the following cognates between Zhangzhung and Proto-West Himalayish.<ref>Widmer, Manuel. 2014. ==Scripts==
A number of scripts are recorded as being used for writing the Zhangzhung language. These are the [[Marchen script]] and its several descendants:<ref>{{cite web | last=West | first=Andrew | author-link=Andrew West (linguist) | title=N4032: Proposal to encode the Marchen script in the SMP of the UCS | url=https://www.unicode.org/L2/L2011/11140-n4032-marchen.pdf | date=30 April 2011 }}</ref>

* [[Marchen script|Marchen]] or Greater Mar script ({{bo|t=སྨར་ཆེན་|w=smar chen}})<ref name="N4491">{{cite web|url=https://www.unicode.org/L2/L2013/13197-marchen.pdf|title=N4491: Final proposal to encode the Marchen script in the SMP of the UCS|date=2013-10-22|first=Andrew|last=West}}</ref>
** [[Marchung script|Marchung]] or Lesser Mar script ({{bo|t=སྨར་ཆུང་|w=smar chung}})
** [[Pungchen script|Pungchen]] or Greater Pung script ({{bo|t=སྤུངས་ཆེན་|w=spungs chen}})
** [[Pungchung script|Pungchung]] or Lesser Pung script ({{bo|t=སྤུངས་ཆུང་|w=spungs chung}})
** [[Drusha script]] ({{bo|t=བྲུ་ཤ་|w=bru sha}})

== Old Zhangzhung ==
[[Frederick William Thomas (philologist)|F. W. Thomas]] suggested that three undeciphered [[Dunhuang manuscripts]] in a Tibetan script were written in an older form of the Zhangzhung language.<ref>{{cite journal | given = F. W. | surname = Thomas | title = The Z̀aṅ-z̀uṅ language | journal = The Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland | year = 1933 | number = 2 | pages = 405–410 |  volume=65|doi = 10.1017/S0035869X00074943 | jstor = 25194777 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | given = F. W. | surname = Thomas | title = The Z̀aṅ-z̀uṅ language | journal = Asia Major | year = 1967 | volume = 13 | number = 1 | pages = 211–217 | url = http://www2.ihp.sinica.edu.tw/file/1747mgTpKPp.pdf | archive-date = 2021-12-20 | access-date = 2020-09-29 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20211220112508/http://www2.ihp.sinica.edu.tw/file/1747mgTpKPp.pdf | url-status = dead }}</ref> This identification has been accepted by {{Nihongo|Takeuchi Tsuguhito|武内紹人}}, who called the language "Old Zhangzhung" and added two further manuscripts.<ref name="Takeuchi">{{cite book | given = Tsuguhito | surname = Takeuchi | chapter = The Old Zhangzhung Manuscript Stein Or 8212/188 | title = Medieval Tibeto-Burman Languages | url = https://archive.org/details/medievaltibetobu00beck | url-access = limited | editor = Christopher Beckwith | pages = [https://archive.org/details/medievaltibetobu00beck/page/n21 1]–11 | location = Leiden | publisher = Brill | year = 2002 | isbn = 978-90-04-12424-0 }}</ref>
Two of these manuscripts are in the Stein collection of the [[British Library]] (IOL Tib J 755 (Ch. Fragment 43) and Or.8212/188) and three in the Pelliot collection of the [[Bibliothèque Nationale]] (Pelliot tibétain 1247, 1251 and 1252).  In each case, the relevant text is written on the reverse side of a scroll containing an earlier Chinese Buddhist text.<ref name="Takeuchi"/>
The texts are written in a style of Tibetan script dating from the late 8th or early 9th centuries.
Takeuchi and Nishida claim to have partially deciphered the documents, which they believe to be separate medical texts.<ref>{{cite book | chapter = The Present Stage of Deciphering Old Zhangzhung | given1 = Tsuguhito | surname1 = Takeuchi | given2 = Ai | surname2 = Nishida | pages = 151–165 | title = Issues in Tibeto-Burman Historical Linguistics | editor-given = Yasuhiko | editor-surname = Nagano | series = Senri Ethnological Studies | volume = 75 | year = 2009 | chapter-url = https://minpaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=repository_uri&item_id=2570&file_id=18&file_no=1 | type = PDF }}</ref>
However, [[David Snellgrove]], and more recently Dan Martin, have rejected Thomas's identification of the language of these texts as a variant of Zhangzhung.<ref>{{cite journal | surname = Snellgrove | given = David L. | year = 1959 | title = Review of Giuseppe Tucci, ''Preliminary Report on Two Scientific Expeditions in Nepal'', Serie Orientale Roma no. 10, Istituto Italiano per il Medio ed Estremo Oriente (Rome 1956) | journal = Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London | volume = 22 | issue = 2 | pages = 377–378 | doi = 10.1017/S0041977X00068944 | jstor = 609450 | s2cid = 190715371 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | given = Dan | surname = Martin | title = Knowing Zhang-zhung: the very idea | journal = Journal of the International Association for Bon Research | volume = 1 | year = 2013 | pages = 175–197 | url = https://himalaya.socanth.cam.ac.uk/collections/journals/jiabr/pdf/JIABR_01_10.pdf | archive-date = 2024-06-29 | access-date = 2025-10-22 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20240629192206/https://himalaya.socanth.cam.ac.uk/collections/journals/jiabr/pdf/JIABR_01_10.pdf | url-status = dead }}</ref>
